Lancashire
LANG-kuh-shur
n. (the north-western English county that remained the most recusant in the kingdom and at the same time bred the strongest northern Puritanism)
From Lancaster, the Roman camp on the Lune, from the river name and Old English ceaster, a fortified town; with scir, a shire.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lancashire is the county between the Mersey and the Lune, and it is the sharpest division in English religious geography. Through the whole of Elizabeth's reign and long after, its gentry held to Rome in greater numbers than anywhere else in England; the Commission for Causes Ecclesiastical reported whole hundreds where the old service was kept in private houses, seminary priests moved between the halls of the Catholic families, and the recusancy fines fell on the same names for generations. Yet the same county produced the most vigorous Puritanism in the north. Bolton was called the Geneva of the north; Manchester's collegiate church had a succession of preaching wardens; Richard Mather of Lowton, Henry Newcome of Manchester and the Lancashire classis of the sixteen-forties made the county a stronghold of Presbyterian order, and the Lancashire ministers subscribed a harmonious consent to the Westminster standards. After 1662 its dissent was numerous and stubborn. The dictionary records the county as a place where two religions lived side by side in one shire for a century and a half, and it names the duty that arises in such a place, which is doctrinal separation without personal malice.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a recusant as one who refuses conformity; a heretic as one who holds an error in the fundamentals of religion; to withdraw as to retire or take back; a classis as an assembly of elders; and separation as the act of parting.

expand to see more

RECUSANT, n. One who refuses communion with the church of England; a nonconformist; particularly a Roman Catholic.

HERETIC, n. A person under any religion, but particularly the Christian, who holds and teaches opinions repugnant to the established faith.

WITHDRAW, v.t. To take back; to recall; to retire; to retreat from a place or from company.

CLASSIS, n. An assembly or body of ministers and elders exercising jurisdiction over several churches.

SEPARATION, n. The act of separating; disjunction; the state of being apart or divided.

Key Scripture

Gal 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

Tit 3:10 — "A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;"

2Th 3:6 — "Now we command you, brethren, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly, and not after the tradition which he received of us."

2Jn 1:10 — "If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed:"

Modern Corruption

North-western county that held more recusant gentry than any other in England while breeding the strongest northern Puritanism, with Bolton called the Geneva of the north.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the gospel of Rome, and the dictionary names it as another gospel rather than as a variant of the same one, because that is the only category Paul leaves available. A religion of the mass as a propitiatory sacrifice, of merit, of a treasury of satisfactions and of a priesthood interposed between a man and his Mediator is not a different emphasis within the faith but a substitution for it, and the apostolic sentence is passed without qualification: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8). Lancashire's Protestant ministers were not uncharitable for holding this; they were holding what Galatians says.

The second paragraph is about conduct, because a county where the two religions were neighbours put the question practically, and the dictionary answers it from the texts that govern it rather than from sentiment. Separation is commanded and it is ecclesiastical: an obstinate man is to be refused after due admonition, for “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10); the disorderly brother is to be withdrawn from, since Paul commands “that ye withdraw yourselves from every brother that walketh disorderly” (2Th 3:6); and the teacher of a false Christ is not to be received as a teacher, for if a man “bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed” (2Jn 1:10). None of this licenses informing, fining or dispossessing a neighbour, and the recusancy statutes did all three. The dictionary holds the doctrine and refuses the apparatus of persecution that Protestant Lancashire used to enforce it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek anathema (G331), accursed; Greek hairetikos (G141), factious or heretical; Greek stello (G4724), to withdraw.

expand to see more

Greek anathema (G331) — a thing devoted to destruction, accursed; “let him be accursed”, Galatians 1:8.

Greek euangelizo (G2097) — to announce good news, to preach a gospel; “preach any other gospel unto you”, Galatians 1:8.

Greek hairetikos (G141) — factious, given to party divisions, heretical; “A man that is an heretick”, Titus 3:10.

Greek stello (G4724) — to set in order, to restrain, to withdraw; “that ye withdraw yourselves”, 2 Thessalonians 3:6.

Greek didache (G1322) — teaching, doctrine; “and bring not this doctrine”, 2 John 10.

Usage

"“let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8) — the mass kept in the halls of the Lancashire gentry."

"“A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10) — separation as ecclesiastical, not civil."

"“receive him not into your house” (2Jn 1:10) — the seminary priests moving between houses."
